name: Kātyāyanīputra

tradition.text: Three hundred years after the parinirvāṇa (Xuanzang)

places: Tāmasavana monastery, Cīnabhukti (per Xuanzang; low confidence)
summary: Author of the Jñānaprasthāna, the root text of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma; the Vaibhāṣikas held that he gathered the Buddha's scattered Abhidharma teachings into a treatise.

name: Vasumitra

tradition.text: Presided over the council of Kaniṣka in Kashmir (Xuanzang)

summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā, who held that dharmas are called past, present and future according to their state (avasthā) — the view Vasubandhu judged the best (AK 5.26). The tradition also credits a Vasumitra with the Prakaraṇapāda and the Samayabhedoparacanacakra; scholars usually distinguish several Vasumitras.
notes: Homonyms: scholars distinguish the Vibhāṣā master, the author of the Prakaraṇapāda and the doxographer; the tradition often identifies them. One id is used here with that caveat.

name: Ghoṣaka
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: dharmas differ in the three times by their characteristic (lakṣaṇa) — a past dharma has the past characteristic without being dissociated from the future and present ones, as a man attached to one woman is not without attachment to others (AKBh 5.26). The Abhidharmāmṛtarasa is attributed to him.

name: Dharmatrāta
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: dharmas passing through the three times change their mode of being (bhāva) but not their substance, as a gold vessel broken and remade (AKBh 5.26). Yaśomitra credits an elder Dharmatrāta with arranging the Udānavarga; he is also counted among the Dārṣṭāntikas.

name: Buddhadeva
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: a dharma is called past, present or future relative to what precedes and follows it, as one woman is called daughter and mother (anyathānyathika, AKBh 5.26).

name: Devaśarman

tradition.text: A hundred years after the parinirvāṇa (Chinese tradition; low confidence)

summary: Author of the Vijñānakāya, one of the six 'feet' of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma, which refutes the denial of past and future and the doctrine of the person.

name: Dharmaśrī
summary: Author of the Abhidharmahṛdaya, the first verse digest of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma.

name: Upaśānta
summary: Commentator on the Abhidharmahṛdaya.

name: Dharmatrāta (author of the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya)
summary: Gandhāran master who enlarged Dharmaśrī's Abhidharmahṛdaya with Vibhāṣā material; distinct from the Vibhāṣā master of the same name.

name: Saṅghabhadra

realization_account.text: Xuanzang relates that he spent twelve years composing a refutation of the Kośa and set out to debate Vasubandhu, who declined; Saṅghabhadra died before they met and Vasubandhu renamed his work Nyāyānusāra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great Kashmiri Vaibhāṣika who defended orthodoxy against Vasubandhu's Sautrāntika criticisms in the Nyāyānusāra, developing new formulations (e.g. on the activity of dharmas).

name: Skandhila
summary: Author of the Abhidharmāvatāra, a concise Vaibhāṣika manual.

name: Yaśomitra
summary: Author of the Sphuṭārthā, the only complete Sanskrit commentary on the Kośa and bhāṣya, written from a Sautrāntika standpoint.

name: Śamathadeva
summary: Compiler of the Upāyikā, which gives in full the sūtras quoted in the Kośa.

name: Pārśva (Sarvāstivāda elder)

realization_account.text: An elder who vowed not to lie down until he had mastered the Tripiṭaka and attained the three knowledges ('the rib elder'); he urged Kaniṣka to convene the Kashmir council.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Sarvāstivāda elder of Gandhāra credited by Xuanzang with prompting the Kashmir council that compiled the Vibhāṣā; distinct from the Jain Tīrthaṅkara Pārśva.

name: Upagupta

tradition.text: A hundred years after the parinirvāṇa, teacher of King Aśoka (Aśokāvadāna)

realization_account.text: He subdued Māra and made him display the Buddha's form; he taught Aśoka; a cave was filled with the tally-sticks of those he led to arhatship.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Master of Mathurā, fourth in the Sarvāstivāda succession after Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda and Śāṇakavāsin, and a hero of the Aśokāvadāna.

name: Śāṇakavāsin
summary: Disciple of Ānanda and teacher of Upagupta in the Sarvāstivāda succession of masters.

name: Madhyāntika

realization_account.text: A disciple of Ānanda who subdued the nāga of the lake of Kashmir and established the Dharma there (northern sources); in the Pali chronicles, one of the missionaries sent after the Third Council to Kashmir-Gandhāra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The legendary bringer of the Dharma to Kashmir.

name: Vasubandhu

realization_account.text: He studied the Vibhāṣā in Kashmir, composed the Kośa verses which the Kashmiris welcomed, then the bhāṣya which criticized them from the Sautrāntika side; later his brother Asaṅga turned him to the Mahāyāna.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author of the Abhidharmakośa and its bhāṣya, the classic summary of Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika Abhidharma with Sautrāntika criticisms; in its ninth chapter he refutes the Vātsīputrīya person and the non-Buddhist self. (This unit contributes the Abhidharma side; the Yogācāra works belong to U41.)

name: Kumāralāta
summary: Called by Xuanzang the 'original master' (founder) of the Sautrāntika; author of the Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti, a collection of illustrative stories.

name: Śrīlāta
summary: Sautrāntika master whose lost Vibhāṣā is known through Saṅghabhadra's refutations; he taught a 'subsidiary element' (anudhātu) carrying the potential of past actions (low confidence on the term).

name: Harivarman
summary: Author of the Satyasiddhiśāstra; trained in the Sarvāstivāda but rejected many of its positions; his school affiliation is variously given as Sautrāntika or Bahuśrutīya.

name: Bhāviveka
summary: Madhyamaka master (U40). This unit records only the doxography of the eighteen schools ascribed to Bhavya in the Tibetan canon.

name: Vinītadeva
summary: Commentator on Dharmakīrti and on Vinaya texts; author of the summary of the eighteen schools in four groups followed in Tibet.

name: Guṇaprabha
summary: Author of the Vinayasūtra; with Śākyaprabha counted in Tibet as one of the 'two supreme ones' of the Vinaya.

name: Mahādeva (of the five points)
alt_names: Dazhongtian 大眾天 / Datian 大天

tradition.text: At the time of the first schism under Aśoka (Vasumitra); a second Mahādeva at the end of the second century founded the Caitika

realization_account.text: The Sarvāstivāda Mahāvibhāṣā tells that Mahādeva, a merchant's son of Mathurā, committed three deadly sins, became a monk at Pāṭaliputra, claimed arhatship and proclaimed five points lowering the arhat, which split the order; this is a hostile account.
realization_account.label: an opponent's account

summary: The monk to whom Vasumitra and the Mahāvibhāṣā attribute the five points on the arhat that caused the first schism; the Mahāsāṃghika sources do not present him so. The Pali tradition knows a different Mahādeva as a missionary.
notes: Reported mainly by the Sarvāstivāda (an opponent).

name: Vātsīputra
summary: Eponymous founder of the Vātsīputrīya, the first Pudgalavāda school; Chinese sources make him a disciple in the line of Śāriputra and Rāhula (low confidence).

name: Dharmagupta
alt_names: Fahu 法護 / Tanwude 曇無德
summary: Eponymous founder of the Dharmaguptaka; Vasumitra says the school claimed Maudgalyāyana as its teacher.

name: Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta

realization_account.text: Finding the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī accepting gold and silver, he objected, was expelled by them, and gathered the elders (Revata, Sabbakāmī and others) for the council that rejected the ten points.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The monk who, according to the Vinaya accounts, called the Second Council at Vaiśālī a century after the parinirvāṇa.

name: Gautama Saṅghadeva
alt_names: Qutan Sengqietipo 瞿曇僧伽提婆
summary: Kashmiri translator of the Madhyamāgama (397–398) and of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma texts.

name: Buddhayaśas
summary: Kashmiri Dharmaguptaka master who recited the Four-Part Vinaya and the Dīrghāgama for translation.

name: Zhu Fonian
summary: Chinese translator who rendered into Chinese the texts recited by Buddhayaśas, Dharmanandi and others.

name: Guṇabhadra
summary: Central Indian translator of the Saṃyuktāgama (435–443) and of the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra.

name: Dharmanandi
summary: Tokharian monk who recited the Ekottarikāgama for translation (384–385).

name: Faxian
summary: Chinese pilgrim who went to India in search of the Vinaya, obtained the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya at Pāṭaliputra and the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya and Āgama manuscripts in Sri Lanka, and translated the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya with Buddhabhadra.

name: Buddhabhadra
summary: Kashmiri meditation master and translator (the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya with Faxian; also the Avataṃsaka).

name: Buddhajīva
summary: Kashmiri Mahīśāsaka monk who translated the Five-Part Vinaya (423–424).

name: Puṇyatāra
summary: Kashmiri master who recited the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya for Kumārajīva's translation (404); he died before it was finished.

name: Kumārajīva
summary: The great Kuchean translator (344–413 or 350–409). This unit records his translations of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya and of the Satyasiddhiśāstra; his Madhyamaka and Mahāyāna work belongs to other units.

name: Xuanzang
summary: Chinese pilgrim and translator (602–664). This unit records his translations of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma (the seven books, the Mahāvibhāṣā in 200 fascicles, the Kośa, the Nyāyānusāra), Vasumitra's doxography, and his record of the schools in India.

name: Paramārtha
summary: Indian translator in China (499–569). This unit records his translation of the Kośa (563–567), of Vasumitra's doxography, of a Saṃmitīya Vinaya treatise, and his Life of Vasubandhu.

name: Yijing
summary: Chinese pilgrim who studied at Nālandā and translated much of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya; his record describes the four nikāyas of India.

name: Daoxuan
summary: Founder of the Nanshan Vinaya school on Mount Zhongnan, who made the Four-Part Vinaya the standard monastic code of China; also a historian (Xu gaoseng zhuan).

name: Jianzhen

realization_account.text: After five failed crossings and the loss of his sight he reached Japan, conferred the precepts at Tōdaiji and founded Tōshōdaiji.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Chinese Vinaya master who established formal ordination by the Four-Part Vinaya in Japan.
notes: Daoxuan listed as teacher in the lineage sense (Nanshan line), not personally.

name: Śāntarakṣita
summary: Nālandā abbot (8th c.). This unit records that he ordained the first Tibetan monks at Samye according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, the origin of the 'lower Vinaya' lineage.

name: Śākyaśrībhadra
summary: Kashmiri master who came to Tibet in 1204 and began the 'Kashmiri paṇḍita' Mūlasarvāstivāda ordination lineage, transmitted in the Sakya and other schools.

name: Lachen Gongpa Rabsal
alt_names: bla chen dgongs pa rab gsal
summary: Tibetan monk in Amdo who preserved the monastic ordination after the persecution of Langdarma; source of the 'lower Vinaya' (smad 'dul) lineage.

name: Tāranātha
summary: Jonang master (1575–1634); this unit records his History of Buddhism in India with its accounts of the councils and schools.
